# Hard-to-vary report: the Time Traveller's fourth-dimension argument

(H. G. Wells, *The Time Machine*, opening chapters)

## 1. The question, frozen

What is being explained: why deliberate travel through time — forward, backward, at a chosen rate — should be *possible* for a machine, given that everyone agrees we normally move through time only one way, at one fixed rate. This is the Traveller's own framing: "this is the object of my investigations," a machine "that shall travel indifferently in any direction of Space and Time." It is a "why can it happen" question, the mirror of a block: common sense says movement in time is shut off, and the argument tries to open the door. Range: it covers whether such movement is possible in principle, and how the model's vanishing should be read. It does not cover how the physical parts of the device work, nor the social consequences raised later at dinner.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **P1 Four dimensions.** Any real body has Length, Breadth, Thickness, and Duration; time is "only another way of looking at" a fourth, space-like dimension.
- **P2 Uniform velocity of consciousness.** Our minds travel along the time-dimension at a fixed rate, cradle to grave — this is offered as the whole reason time *feels* different from space.
- **P3 The balloon analogy.** We once had no free vertical movement (gravity); we built balloons and got some. Likewise we might learn to alter our drift along time.
- **P4 The machine.** Levers said to speed, slow, or reverse that drift.
- **P5 The vanishing demonstration.** The model disappears when the lever is pressed; offered as the evidence.
- **P6 "Diluted presentation" (a patch).** Introduced only after Filby objects that a machine travelling into the *past* should have sat visibly in the room every earlier Thursday: the reply is that it was always there, just moving too fast through time to leave more than an unnoticed trace — like a spinning spoke or a flying bullet.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| P1, four dimensions | Loose | Swap "time is a dimension exactly like the other three" for "time is a distinct order we happen to live through in sequence," and the shadow and barometer illustrations work exactly as well. Nothing in them forces the stronger reading. |
| P2, uniform velocity | Held if | It is needed to license P4 (a machine could speed up or reverse the drift) — but only if "moving at a velocity" is more than a way of saying "getting older." That reading is the Traveller's own addition, not something the geometry argument established. |
| P3, balloon analogy | Loose | Swap "balloon beat gravity" for "ship learned to sail against the current," and the argument's force (technology has beaten apparent limits before) survives unchanged. The example is decoration; what is held is a weak general form that, by itself, proves nothing about *this* limit. |
| P4, the machine | Unknown | No poke in the excerpt separates "the levers alter time-drift" from "the levers are a stage prop." The one piece of evidence is P5, which is exactly the thing in dispute. |
| P5, the vanishing | Borrowed | It rests on the narrator's word that "there was no trickery" — an assertion, not a test. The Medical Man names the rival at once ("some sleight-of-hand trick... like that ghost you showed us last Christmas"), and nothing on show tells the two apart. |
| P6, diluted presentation | Idle as a prediction, held only as a patch | It appears the instant a counter-case (the visible-every-Thursday problem) threatens the theory, and it has no other job than absorbing that one objection: a catch-all with no gauge, since nothing is proposed that would show whether presentation-below-threshold is really happening or is just being said. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** Had the model simply sat inert, would the four-dimension theory count as refuted, or merely "not yet demonstrated"? The text gives no way to tell — a theory that survives either outcome equally explains neither.
- **Direction.** The whole case runs backward from one witnessed effect (a vanishing) to a cause (time travel), with no attempt to poke the supposed cause and watch the effect respond independently.
- **Answer hidden in the starting points.** "Our mental existence... passing along the Time-Dimension with a uniform velocity" already contains, under another name, the very thing the machine is meant to demonstrate: that the rate is a real, alterable quantity, not just a figure of speech for ageing.
- **Rivals.** The stage-trick hypothesis and the Traveller's account respond identically to everything shown (a draught, a flash, an object gone). At this level the excerpt has not told them apart.
- **Where the jobs came from.** The main job — make time travel intelligible — is *given* (it is what the Traveller sets out to do). The secondary job of explaining invisibility-during-transit (P6) is *added*, invented on the spot by the Psychologist in reply to a listener's objection, not predicted by the theory beforehand.
- **Where the parts came from.** P1, P2, P3 and P6 are all *asserted* — declared by a speaker and not tested against anything within the scene. None is *built* (worked out with the machine itself in view and then set against a case that could have broken it) or *fitted* (tuned against a run of past trials, even a fictional one).

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

Two changes would tighten this a great deal. First, a poke that could fail: some named change to the demonstration — weight the model, put an obstacle in its path, have a sceptic press the lever from across the room — with a stated prediction for "theory true" and a different one for "trick." Second, an independent reason for P6 that is not invented at the moment it is needed: a prediction, made before Filby's objection, of exactly how faint or brief the machine's presence in ordinary time should look, checkable against something already on record rather than supplied to save the story once the gap is spotted.

## 6. What this does not show

This is not a verdict on whether the chapters are well written, nor on whether time travel is possible. It only asks whether the Traveller's argument, as given here, is held in place by anything checkable inside the scene. A loose argument can still sit inside a good story — indeed the story's own point, so far, is that the other guests are *right* to withhold belief until harder evidence turns up.

## 7. One next step

Read on to the Traveller's return with mud, a limp, and (later) a wilted, unknown flower, and run the same tests on that evidence. Does it pass "build the best rival" (a bad night wandering at home, versus a trip through time) any better than the model demonstration did?
